inline_text:
### Project Name

legacy2mcp

### Project Description

legacy2mcp turns legacy enterprise systems (SOAP/WSDL services, relational databases and older REST APIs) into MCP servers that AI agents can use safely. You point it at a WSDL, a database or an API, and it generates typed MCP tools without anyone writing adapter code by hand.

How it works:
- It reads the legacy system directly (every operation in a WSDL, or the live schema of a database) and builds a JSON Schema for each tool from what it finds.
- Every tool call is validated against that schema before anything is sent to the backend.
- It's read-only out of the box. Write-like operations are left out unless you turn them on, and the database adapter only allows tables and named, parameterized queries you list in config. The LLM never gets to run its own SQL.
- Every call is written to an audit log.
- `legacy2mcp init` can scan an existing codebase (SOAP clients, ORM models, Flask/FastAPI routes) and draft a starter config for you.
- New system types plug in through a small `BaseAdapter` interface (`discover_tools()` and `invoke()`). The core takes care of validation, dispatch and logging.

Why it matters: a lot of important business data still lives behind SOAP services and direct database access. Teams that want to put agents on top of those systems usually end up hand-writing fragile glue code or giving the agent far more access than it needs. I wanted the safe option to also be the easy one.

Background: I started legacy2mcp after spending 14+ years building web service integrations (both REST and SOAP) and the last couple of years working on agentic systems. The repo went public in September 2026. v0.1.0 shipped the SOAP/WSDL adapter, v0.2 added the database adapter (Postgres, SQL Server and Oracle), and v0.2.x added a REST adapter and the `init` command. The current release is v0.2.1. It's on PyPI and in the official MCP Registry as `io.github.bvenkata/legacy2mcp`.

### Alignment with AAIF Mission

As I understand it, AAIF exists to give the protocols and tools that let agents work together a neutral, open home, with a strong focus on doing that safely. legacy2mcp fits that in a few ways:
- It's built on MCP. It uses the official `mcp` Python SDK and its whole job is to produce standard MCP servers, which brings a big set of older enterprise systems into the MCP ecosystem.
- Safety is the default, not an add-on. Schema validation, read-only mode, allowlists and audit logging are on from the start.
- It isn't tied to any vendor. The servers work with any MCP client, and the optional LLM help in `init` works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
- It's Apache-2.0 and designed so other people can add adapters for systems I haven't covered.

### Relation to Existing AAIF Projects

- Model Context Protocol (MCP): legacy2mcp is an MCP implementation. It generates MCP servers over stdio today, with HTTP/SSE planned, and it's listed in the MCP Registry. I'd like it to become a good reference for how to connect legacy systems through MCP without opening up too much access.
- goose and other MCP hosts: any MCP-capable agent, goose included, can use the servers legacy2mcp produces with no changes.
- AGENTS.md: these sit next to each other well. AGENTS.md helps agents understand a codebase, and legacy2mcp gives those agents controlled access to the backend systems that code talks to.

I'm not aware of any overlap with existing AAIF projects.

### Example Use Cases and Evidence of Adoption

Some of the ways it can be used:
- Systems of record: an agent looks up status and detail records in an old back-office system. Read-only, and every lookup is logged.
- Financial services: let an agent read accounts and transactions while transfers and adjustments stay off limits.
- Supply chain and ERP: expose order status, inventory and shipment tracking from older SOAP middleware.
- Internal support tools: give a support assistant typed access to the real system instead of having it scrape a UI.
- Modernization: put an MCP layer in front of a legacy service now and replace the backend later without touching the agent.
- CI/CD: run tool discovery in the pipeline to catch WSDL changes before they hit production.

On adoption, I want to be upfront: this is an early project and I'm applying for Sandbox. It's published on PyPI, in the official MCP Registry and on Glama, but I can't point to production deployments at multiple organizations yet. Growing adoption and bringing in maintainers from other companies are a big part of why I'm applying.

### Governance Model

Right now it's a single-maintainer project and I make the final calls. If accepted, I plan to move to the LF Minimum Viable Governance model, add GOVERNANCE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, and bring on maintainers from other organizations.

### CI/CD & Release Workflow

CI runs on GitHub Actions (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) for every push and pull request to `main`. It tests on Python 3.10, 3.11 and 3.12, runs the full pytest suite, checks that WSDL to MCP tool discovery still works, and makes sure the bundled demo configs (Orders and Petstore) still generate tools.

Releases are handled by `.github/workflows/release.yml`. Pushing a version tag (`v*`) builds the package, publishes it to PyPI using trusted publishing, waits for it to show up, then publishes the server entry to the MCP Registry with `mcp-publisher`.

I cut releases as features are ready (v0.1.0 through v0.2.x so far) and follow semantic versioning. There's also a Dockerfile, a docker-compose setup and a demo SOAP service for trying it locally.

### Public-Facing Contribution Process for Specifications

legacy2mcp is a tool, not a spec, so there isn't a separate spec process. Changes go through public GitHub issues and pull requests at https://github.com/bvenkata/legacy2mcp. New adapters are the most useful thing people can contribute. For bigger design changes I'd open an issue first so it can be discussed in public before any code is written. I'll be adding a CONTRIBUTING.md that spells this out.

### Roadmap

The roadmap is public here: https://github.com/bvenkata/legacy2mcp/blob/main/docs/roadmap.md

Done:
- v0.1: SOAP/WSDL adapter, schema generation, validation, read-only default, audit log, `run` and `inspect` commands, basic auth, stdio
- v0.2: database adapter for Postgres, SQL Server and Oracle, with allowlists and named parameterized queries
- v0.2.x: REST adapter with an endpoint allowlist, plus `legacy2mcp init` to generate configs

Next 12 months:
- HTTP/SSE transport, role-based tool authorization, OAuth2 for SOAP
- Queue adapters (Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS)
- Workflow composition with approval steps
- OpenTelemetry export

### Security

There's no OpenSSF Best Practices badge yet. I plan to apply for one.

Where things stand today:
- Read-only by default. Write-like SOAP operations are excluded unless you opt in, and database access is limited to tables and named, parameterized queries you explicitly allow. No free-form SQL.
- Every call is checked against its JSON Schema before it reaches the backend, and every call is logged.
- I've documented the known gaps in docs/security.md: the SOAP write filter works off operation names so it can miss things, there's no column-level masking, and the MCP server itself doesn't have auth yet. Role-based authorization and OAuth2 are on the roadmap.
- Releases go to PyPI through trusted publishing from GitHub Actions.
